title: eAudit: A Fast, Scalable and Deployable Audit Data Collection System
used_for: Step 6's workloads and metrics (ADR-0018); step 2b's ceiling gate (the cost of one ring-buffer record per event); the tamper-window metric
key_claims_used: Hooks: syscall enter/exit tracepoints only, 80 syscalls (Table 1), BCC, 16 MB ring buffer (§3.2-3.3, §4). Records 17 bytes on average on postmark against 175 (sysdig) and 850 (auditd) (§3.4). Two-level buffer: a per-CPU message cache of p records flushed to the ring buffer, the consumer woken once per w messages; defaults p=100, w=8; without the cache (p=1) up to 60% loss, none at p>=18 on 12 cores (§3.5, Fig. 8-9). Model: buffering cost per event (tq + ts/w)/p; measured tq 0.77 us and ts 2.85 us on 12 cores, 2.26 us and 20.6 us on 2 cores (Table 11, Fig. 12). Priorities: a weight per syscall class forces an immediate flush for exec, setuid, kill, ptrace; nothing is held longer than 2^24 ns (§3.7). Results: no loss on any benchmark at 1-12 cores, rdwr about 17 M syscalls/s (§4.1); agent overhead (agent CPU / benchmark CPU) 3.1% on average, median 48 ns per syscall (§4.3, Fig. 18-19); wall-clock overhead under 30% for all but rdwr, 18% on average, 5.8% without find, tar and rdwr (§4.4); 4-5% on postmark and shbm against 39-65% (sysdig, CamFlow) and 118-900% (auditd, Tracee, Tetragon) (Fig. 20); tamper window 355-940 records against 3,479-702,277 for sysdig, 2-11 critical records (Table 22); logs 10.8x smaller than sysdig's uncompressed, 5.8x gzipped (Tables 23-24). Benchmarks: postmark, shbm, find, tar, rdwr, httperf, kernel build (Table 5). Stated limits: LRU maps for state; at most 32 execve arguments; not evaluated for detection
